title: Directing sidemen as a leader and studio adjustments
summary: McBee describes asking players to adjust parts in the studio, such as sustaining chords or laying out.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: Yeah. Let me ask you a question about when you have recorded as a leader, I wonder if you’ve ever had a situation where you needed to tell someone in the group to play differently, or not do something, because you collectively write compositions and we have something in our head, and then we hand the parts out to other people, we teach them, and you’re not sure what you’re going to get. So if I go back to my original question, have you ever had to re-direct someone on a recording because you weren’t quite happy with what they were doing?

Sure. Remember you, as a composer, you are the one that has exacted qualities of thought that find, you know, qualities of performances by those that you have chosen. So simply you can ask someone to, like I said before, when I play, when I’m soloing, please sustain the chords. Don’t get rhythmic, don’t get rhythmic because that might interfere with my rhythms when I’m soloing. So if you know, anything can be altered. During a recording things are constantly done, adjusted from time to time. You might want your alto to play an octave lower, or play an octave higher. But then you might want him to play in the middle of the piano. You might want the drums to use brushes etcetera. So there are a lot of adjustments that are made in the studio that would help fashion the final recording, adjustments that would ordinarily be made spontaneously on the stage. At the end of the set you might tell the piano look, why don’t you lay out at that spot and I can have that spot fashion more of what I’m doing rhythmically doing on the bass, then you might enter at Letter B or something. So those things happen all the time.
